extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Kantian aesthetics; readers of philosophical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Expository and annotative material on Kant's Critique of Judgment, giving definitions, distinctions, and examples for understanding and applying Kant's theories of taste, the beautiful, and the sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The definition of taste laid down here is that it is the faculty of judging of the beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis of judgements of taste must show what is required to call an object beautiful; the moments of reflection in such judgement are sought in accordance with the guidance of the logical functions of judgement. The moment of quality is considered first because the aesthetic judgement upon the beautiful first pays attention to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disinterestedness of aesthetic judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement upon an object of satisfaction may be quite disinterested; judgements of taste do not in themselves establish any interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disinterestedness means the judgement is not based upon an interest (not directed to possession or use). Only in society is it 'interesting' to have taste; pure aesthetic judgements should avoid interests or purposes that determine the judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure: practical vs contemplative (taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure necessarily bound up with desire may be called practical pleasure; the pleasure not necessarily bound up with desire is mere contemplative pleasure or passive satisfaction; the feeling of this latter kind of pleasure we call taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical pleasure is linked to desire for the object's existence or use; contemplative pleasure attaches to the representation itself. Taste is the contemplative form and should not be conflated with practical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposiveness without purpose (aesthetic purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: We perceive a certain purposiveness in objects (e.g., a flower) which in our judgement is referred to no purpose at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If we regard a thing as a work of art, we infer a definite purpose and thus no immediate satisfaction; natural beauty gives the sense of purposiveness without reference to a purpose (formal purposiveness), which underlies aesthetic delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for claiming universal assent for aesthetic judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: To justify claiming universal assent for an aesthetical judgement that rests merely on subjective grounds, it is sufficient to assume (1) that the subjective conditions of the judgement ... are the same in all men; and (2) the judgement must merely have reference to this relation (consequently to the formal condition of the judgement) and be pure, i.e. not mingled either with concepts of the object or with sensations as determining grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (1) Common subjective conditions: cognitive powers' relations to cognition in general must be shared so communication is possible. (2) Purity: the judgement must not be contaminated by concepts or particular sensations; if contaminated, this is only an inaccurate application of the privilege, not a refutation of the privilege in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity requirement for aesthetic judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: An aesthetical judgement must be pure — not mingled either with concepts of the object or with sensations as determining grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a judgement is mixed with concepts (e.g., purpose, function) or with sensations tied to desire, then it ceases to be a pure judgement of taste; such mixing produces inaccurate applications of aesthetic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic vs teleological judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic judgements simply regard form with disinterested satisfaction; teleological judgements pay attention to the reference of natural beauty to some purpose and can regard it as a favour of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish when one is appreciating form for its own sake (aesthetic) and when one interprets features as serving purposes (teleological). The latter involves consideration of ends and functions and thus is not pure taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models of taste should be in a dead and learned language
rubrics_metrics.description: Models of taste as regards the arts of speech must be composed in a dead and learned language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: dead languages avoid inevitable change that living languages undergo; learned languages have grammar preserved from fashion. This is a practical recommendation for canonical taste-models to retain stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature as violation of the normal Idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The exaggeration of a characteristic which does violence to the normal Idea (the purposiveness of the race) is called caricature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A perfectly regular countenance often tells nothing characteristic; exaggeration departs from the ordinary relations of mental powers and thereby produces caricature. Caricature expresses what is characteristic by departing from normal proportion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affections vs passions distinction and aesthetic relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Affections are specifically different from passions: the former are related merely to feeling; the latter belong to the faculty of desire and are inclinations which render difficult or impossible determination of the will by principles. Affections are hasty and unpremeditated; passions are steady and deliberate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passions can never be called sublime because in a passion the freedom of the mind is abolished; in an affection freedom is only hindered. For aesthetic assessment, only affections can figure into the sublime (where freedom is not abolished).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublime: modified pain/terror can produce delight
rubrics_metrics.description: If the pain and terror are so modified as not to be actually noxious ... they are capable of producing delight; not pleasure, but a sort of delightful horror, a sort of tranquillity tinged with terror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Burke: the sublime involves an admixture of awe/terror that, when kept from true harm, yields a high form of delight; this explains how experiences of the sublime can be pleasurable without being comfortable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste involves reference to the Understanding (formal relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a judgement of taste a reference to the Understanding is always involved; I have considered the moment of quality first, because the aesthetic judgement upon the beautiful first pays attention to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgement is not purely sensory; it engages cognitive faculties and their formal relations. Evaluations of beauty should account for this interplay between imagination and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensus communis aestheticus (common sense) as basis for taste
rubrics_metrics.description: We may designate Taste as sensus communis aestheticus, common Understanding as sensus communis logicus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taste appeals to a shared 'aesthetic common sense' — a faculty enabling communicable judgements of taste. Appeals to taste should presuppose some common ground in cognitive faculties among observers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetoric vs beautiful art — distinction in evaluative esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Readiness and accuracy in speaking (rhetoric) belong to beautiful art; but the art of the orator (ars oratoria) — availing oneself of the weaknesses of men for one's own designs — is worthy of no respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating speech or literary art, distinguish aesthetic qualities (clarity, imagination, impression) from rhetorical art used to manipulate; the latter may be effective but is morally and aesthetically suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of arts by relation to purposiveness and imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Landscape gardening may be regarded as a species of the art of painting ... since it actually takes its forms from nature ... and involves merely the free play of the Imagination in contemplation, it so far agrees with mere aesthetical painting which has no definite theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When classifying or evaluating arts, consider whether their forms are derived from nature and whether they prompt free play of imagination (aesthetic painting) or are bound by concepts/purposes (architecture). This yields criteria for grouping arts under aesthetic principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold (trichotomy) structure for synthetic a priori divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: If a priori division is to be derived from a priori concepts ... the division must necessarily be trichotomy: (1) a condition, (2) a conditioned, and (3) the concept which arises from the union of the conditioned with its condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological principle: where synthetic a priori classifications are required, expect three-part structures. This is a guideline for structuring philosophical analyses and for evaluating whether divisions capture necessary relations.
